questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy presented with a 5-day history of fevers and rash and a 2-day history of swelling of the hands and feet. He had received all childhood vaccinations. He had no recent foreign travel and no sick contacts. He did not attend nursery and was a single child. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C, he had bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, cracked red lips, and a macular perineal rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Kawasaki syndrome Measles is less likely in a vaccinated child. Rubella and parvovirus infection do not involve conjunctiva. SJS would progress with more extensive cutaneous disease. Kawasaki disease typically presents with the above features.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q46

questions.question: An 8-year-old child has 5 days of fever with a polymorphic rash, nausea/vomiting and conjunctivitis. ESR is 85, WBC 12, platelets 330.
questions.question_raw: Kawasaki question – 8 yo kid with 5 day fever and polymorphic rash, N/V, conjunctivitis. ESR 85, WBC 12, Plts 330

parts.text: Name 4 major criteria of Kawasaki disease.
What are 4 other infections to consider?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 other infections to consider

questions.model_answer:
a) Four of the five classic (major) criteria (fever being the fifth): (1) Bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection (no tearing/exudate) (2) Oral mucosal changes (fissured/erythematous lips, strawberry tongue, injected pharynx) (3) Extremity changes (erythema/edema of palms and soles, later periungual desquamation) (4) Polymorphous rash. [Fifth criterion: cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm, usually unilateral.]
b) Infections to exclude: (1) Adenovirus (2) Measles (3) Enterovirus (4) Staphylococcal/streptococcal toxic shock (scarlet fever).
c) Associated clinical features: (1) Myocarditis (present in virtually all patients, may cause a gallop) (2) Non-calculous cholecystitis/gallbladder hydrops (or arthritis, aseptic meningitis, sterile pyuria/urethritis).
d) Treatment: IVIG 2 g/kg plus aspirin, given within the first 10 days of fever (reduces coronary aneurysm risk from ~25% to ~5%); IVIG-resistant disease treated with a second IVIG dose, infliximab, or corticosteroids.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy has fever for 5 days, then presents with a pleomorphic rash, pharyngitis, strawberry tongue and elevated inflammatory markers. You suspect Kawasaki disease.
questions.question_raw: 6-year-old boy has fever for 5 days, then presents to medical attention with a pleomorphic rash, pharyngitis, strawberry tongue and elevated inflammatory markers. You suspect Kawasaki's disease – (2019)

parts.text: Other than fever, what are four diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease?
What are 4 infectious aetiologies that should be excluded?
What are 2 serious complications that can arise from Kawasaki disease?
What are 2 medical therapies used in the treatment of this condition?

parts_raw.text: A) Other than fever, what are four diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki's disease?
B) What are 4 infectious aetiologies that should be excluded?
C) What are 2 serious complications that can arise from Kawasaki's disease?
D) What are 2 medical therapies that are used in the treatment of this condition

questions.model_answer:
a) Four classic criteria (other than fever): (1) Bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection (2) Oral mucosal changes (fissured red lips, strawberry tongue, injected pharynx) (3) Extremity changes (palm/sole erythema and edema, periungual desquamation) (4) Polymorphous rash. [Fifth: cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm.]
b) Infectious aetiologies to exclude: (1) Adenovirus (2) Measles (3) Enterovirus (4) Staphylococcal/streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (scarlet fever). [Also parvovirus B19, RMSF, leptospirosis.]
c) Serious complications: (1) Coronary artery aneurysm (develops in ~25% of untreated children) (2) Myocardial infarction (from aneurysm thrombosis; myocarditis is near-universal).
d) Medical therapies: (1) IVIG 2 g/kg (2) Aspirin. [For IVIG resistance: repeat IVIG, infliximab, or corticosteroids.]

cohort_answer.text: Diagnostic criteria: Bilateral bulbar conjunctival injection; Oral mucous membrane changes (fissured lips, injected pharynx, strawberry tongue); Erythema of palms and soles or periungal desquamation; Polymorphous rash; Cervical lymphadenopathy. Infectious etiologies to exclude: Adenovirus; Measles; EBV; Echovirus. Complications: Coronary artery aneurysm; MI. Therapies: IVIG; Aspirin; Glucocorticoids

questions.question: Kawasaki disease.

parts.text: Other than fever, name the major criteria.

parts_raw.text: Other than fever, name major criteria

questions.model_answer:
a) Major criteria (other than fever): (1) Bilateral non-exudative bulbar conjunctival injection (2) Oral mucosal changes (fissured/red lips, strawberry tongue, injected pharynx) (3) Extremity changes (palm/sole erythema and edema, periungual desquamation) (4) Polymorphous rash (5) Cervical lymphadenopathy >=1.5 cm (usually unilateral, least reliable, seen in only 30-50%).
b) Infectious differentials: (1) Adenovirus (2) Measles (3) Enterovirus (4) Staphylococcal/streptococcal toxic shock (scarlet fever).
c) Complications: (1) Coronary artery aneurysm (2) Myocardial infarction.
d) Treatments: (1) IVIG 2 g/kg (2) Aspirin. [Resistant disease: infliximab or corticosteroids.]

cohort_answer.text: Major criteria: cervical lymphadenopathy (often unilateral), strawberry tongue/buccal mucosa, non-purulent conjunctivitis, macular rash/rash on hands that desquamates (CREAM-F: Conjunctivitis, Rash, Extremity/Adenopathy, Mucosal changes, Fever). Infectious DDx: Toxic Shock (strep or staph), Measles, Adenovirus, EBV, RMSF, COVID MIS-C. Complications: coronary artery aneurysms, MI. Treatments: IVIG, ASA; if not improving, steroids and biologics (infliximab). Diagnosis requires 5 of 6 criteria including fever; incomplete Kawasaki if fever ≥5 days and 2-3 other manifestations.

questions.question: A 9-month-old presents with fever, irritability and hypotension, a diffuse erythematous rash involving the face, trunk and extremities with areas of desquamation and bulla formation, cracked lips but no oral involvement; applying pressure adjacent to a bulla causes it to rupture.
questions.question_raw: You see a 9 month-old child presenting with fever, irritability, and hypotension. They have a diffuse erythematous rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities, with regions of desquamation and bull formation. The lips are cracked but there is no oral involvement. Application of pressure adjacent to a bulla leads to it rupturing.

parts.text: What is the name of the most likely condition?
What is the toxin responsible for this condition?
MIS-C is also on the differential diagnosis. Name TWO organ systems and ONE finding in each system that are on the WHO diagnostic criteria.

parts_raw.text: What is the name of the most likely condition?
What is the toxin responsible for this condition?
MIS-C is also on the differentiation diagnosis. Name TWO organ systems and ONE finding in each system that are on the WHO diagnostic criteria.

questions.model_answer: a) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) - the positive Nikolsky sign (bulla rupture on adjacent pressure) supports this. b) Staphylococcal exfoliative (epidermolytic) toxin - ETA and/or ETB. c) Any two of the WHO MIS-C criteria systems, e.g.: (1) Cardiovascular - hypotension/shock (or myocardial dysfunction/coronary abnormality). (2) Gastrointestinal - abdominal pain, vomiting or diarrhoea. (Other acceptable: mucocutaneous - rash/bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis/mucocutaneous inflammation; coagulation - elevated D-dimer/coagulopathy.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The WHO MIS-C diagnostic criteria are from WHO guidance, not the Mandell chapter.

questions.question: An 8-month-old child has fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, and irritability. There are cracked lips with no other oral involvement, no conjunctivitis, a confluent erythematous rash over the face, trunk, and diaper region, and a positive Nikolsky sign.
questions.question_raw: 8 month old child with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, irritability. Has cracked lips, no other oral involvement. No conjunctivitis. Confluent erythematous rash over face, trunk, and diaper region. Positive Nikolsky sign.

parts.text: What toxin is responsible for this?
MIS-C is on the differential. Name two organ systems involved and one symptom/manifestation for each that would meet the WHO criteria.

parts_raw.text: What toxin is responsible for this (0.5)
MIS-C is on the differential for this patient. Name two organ systems involved and one symptom/manifestation for each that would meet the WHO criteria (2)

questions.model_answer:
a) Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS).
b) Exfoliative (epidermolytic) toxins A and B (eta/etb), serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis.
c) Two organ systems with one qualifying manifestation each: (1) Cardiac - myocardial dysfunction/pericarditis on echocardiography (or coronary artery abnormality). (2) Gastrointestinal - vomiting, diarrhea, or abdominal pain. (Other acceptable systems: mucocutaneous - rash/bilateral conjunctivitis; hematologic - coagulopathy.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The WHO MIS-C case-definition organ systems/criteria are from WHO guidance, not this Mandell page slice.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Toxin: Exfoliative toxin A and B. MIS-C organ systems: Cardiac - pericarditis or cardiac dysfunction on echo; GI - diarrhea, nausea, vomiting; Integumentary - rash/mucocutaneous inflammation of hands/feet
